tip: Question word + και να (ke na) = '-ever': όπως και να το δεις (opos ke na to deis) = however you look at it. Same mold: ό,τι και να (oti ke na) = whatever.
The -οντας (-ontas) ending is Greek's '-ing': συνοψίζοντας (sinopsizondas) = summing up. One word does the job of English 'to sum up'.
Στο κάτω κάτω (sto kato kato) is literally 'at the bottom bottom' – doubled κάτω (kato) is how Greek says 'at the end of the day'.
Greek's 'as… as' is τόσο… όσο (toso… oso): τόσο απλό όσο ακούγεται (toso aplo oso akougetai) = as simple as it sounds.
Conclusions aren't drawn in Greek – they're taken out: βγάλουμε συμπεράσματα (vgaloume symperasmata), from βγάζω (vgazo = take out).
Glue καλο- (kalo = well) onto a verb and it means doing it properly: καλοσκεφτείς (kaloskefteis) = think it over, not just σκεφτείς (skefteis = think).
Εν τέλει (en telei) is the native 'in the end' – the word-for-word English calque στο τέλος της ημέρας (sto telos tis imeras) sounds translated, not Greek.
The double negative English forbids is mandatory here: ούτε υπέρ ούτε κατά (oute yper oute kata = neither for nor against) still needs δεν (den) before the verb.
Αν και (an ke) looks like 'if and' but means 'even though': αν και διαφωνούμε (an ke diafonoume) = even though we disagree. No special verb form follows – just the normal one.
Παρακαλείσθε όπως (parakaleisthe opos) is the frozen official formula for 'you are requested to' – you'll meet it in notices and letters, never in speech.
Διά της παρούσης (dia tis parousis = by the present letter) is the fixed 'hereby' opener of official documents – bureaucratic Greek preserved from the older formal language.
Εκδημία (ekdimia) is the formal euphemism for death in announcements – literally a 'departure from home'. Everyday Greek says θάνατος (thanatos).
Συμβάσεως (symvaseos = of the contract) carries the formal -εως (-eos) genitive; everyday Greek says σύμβασης (symvasis). Contracts and official letters keep the old ending.
Formal invitations say εσπέρα (espera) for evening; everyday Greek says βράδυ (vradi). Wedding and baptism cards run on this elevated register.
Τυγχάνει επεξεργασίας (tynchanei epexergasias = is being processed) is officialese – literally 'it chances upon processing', the bureaucratic way to phrase a plain passive.
Δύνανται (dynantai) is legal-formal for 'they may' – everyday Greek says μπορούν (boroun). Regulations and notices keep the archaic verb.
Θυγατρός (thygatros = of the daughter) is the archaic formal genitive; everyday Greek says της κόρης (tis koris). Birth announcements keep the old form.
Άμα τη δύσει (ama ti dysei) is a fossil: literally 'at the setting', frozen ancient grammar surviving on signs. Everyday Greek would say στη δύση του ήλιου (sti dysi tou iliou).
Αμελλητί (amelliti) is legalese for 'without delay' in a single word; everyday Greek uses the phrase χωρίς καθυστέρηση (choris kathysterisi).
Μεσημβρία (mesimvria) is the formal word for noon – hotel notices use it where everyday Greek says μεσημέρι (mesimeri).
Ουδείς (oudeis) is the formal 'no one' of rules and regulations – everyday Greek says κανείς (kaneis). Seeing it signals you're reading officialese.
Απηύθυνε (apifthine = addressed) marks the formal past inside the verb: ε (e) changes to η (i). The everyday past is απεύθυνε (apefthine).
Εβαπτίσθη (evaptisthi = was baptized) is the formal passive past; everyday Greek says βαφτίστηκε (vaftistike). Church and official announcements keep the -θη (-thi) ending.
Απεκόπη (apekopi = was cut off) is the formal short passive past; everyday speech says αποκόπηκε (apokopike). Essays on art and history favor the compact old form.
Ευρίσκεται (evrisketai) is the formal face of everyday βρίσκεται (vrisketai = is located) – the older ευ- (ev-) beginning survives in brochures and listings.
Ευχόμεθα (efchometha = we wish) keeps the archaic -μεθα (-metha) 'we' ending; everyday Greek says ευχόμαστε (efchomaste). Formal wishes to newlyweds run on it.
Family traits: το μήλο κάτω απ' τη μηλιά θα πέσει (to milo kato ap' ti milia tha pesei) = the apple will fall under its tree – Greek's 'apple doesn't fall far'.
Effort that backfires: πήγε για μαλλί και βγήκε κουρεμένος (pige gia mali ke vgike kouremenos) = he went for wool and came out shorn – hoping to gain, he lost instead.
Wasted advice: στου κουφού την πόρτα όσο θέλεις βρόντα (stou koufou tin porta oso theleis vronta) = knock all you want at the deaf man's door – Greek's 'talking to a wall'.
Patience pays: αγάλι αγάλι γίνεται η αγουρίδα μέλι (agali agali ginetai i agourida meli) = little by little the sour grape becomes honey – slow progress still ripens.
Thrift: φασούλι το φασούλι γεμίζει το σακούλι (fasouli to fasouli gemizei to sakouli) = bean by bean the sack fills up – and the rhyme makes it stick.
Blame-shifting: φωνάζει ο κλέφτης να φοβηθεί ο νοικοκύρης (fonazei o kleftis na fovithei o noikokyris) = the thief shouts to scare the householder – the guilty accuse first.
Too many bosses: όπου λαλούν πολλοί κοκόροι, αργεί να ξημερώσει (opou laloun polloi kokoroi, argei na ximerosei) = where many roosters crow, dawn comes late.
On meddling: όποιος ανακατεύεται με τα πίτουρα, τον τρώνε οι κότες (opios anakatevetai me ta pitoura, ton trone i kotes) = whoever meddles with the bran gets eaten by the hens.
Better safe: κάλλιο γαϊδουρόδενε παρά γαϊδουρογύρευε (kallio gaidourodene para gaidourogireve) = better tie your donkey than go looking for it – prevention beats searching.
Sour grapes, Greek style: όσα δεν φτάνει η αλεπού τα κάνει κρεμαστάρια (osa den ftanei i alepou ta kanei kremastaria) – grapes she can't reach, the fox calls hung-up-to-keep.
On hindsight: στερνή μου γνώση να σ' είχα πρώτα (sterni mou gnosi na s' icha prota) = my late-coming wisdom, if only I'd had you first – addressed to hindsight itself.
Healthy skepticism: όπου ακούς πολλά κεράσια, κράτα και μικρό καλάθι (opou akous polla kerasia, krata ke mikro kalathi) = where you hear of many cherries, carry a small basket too.
On forgetting: όποιος δεν έχει μυαλό, έχει ποδάρια (opios den echei myalo, echei podaria) = whoever has no brains has legs – your feet pay for what your head forgot.
Το να + verb turns an action into a subject: το να παραδεχτείς (to na paradechteis) = admitting, as in 'admitting takes courage'. Greek uses the article where English uses '-ing'.
To contrast explanations Greek uses δεν είναι ότι… είναι ότι… (den einai oti… einai oti…) = it's not that… it's that… – the frame sets up the correction before it lands.
Δεν ήταν η αποτυχία… αλλά (den itan i apotychia… alla = it wasn't the failure… but) fronts the wrong candidate first – Greek's way of spotlighting what really mattered.
Προσποιούμενος (prospoioumenos = pretending) looks passive with its -ούμενος (-oumenos) ending, but the meaning is active – some Greek verbs only wear the passive shape.
An -οντας (-ontas) verb sets the scene for the main clause: διασχίζοντας τα σύνορα (diaschizontas ta synora = crossing the border), I felt… – Greek's 'while doing X' opener.
Μολονότι (molonoti) is the formal 'although'; everyday Greek says αν και (an ke). Same meaning – written and literary Greek just prefers the heavier word.
